job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Karl Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a rented room in a terrace in Gannet Bay with my mate Tobias, who works nights at the docks, so the house is quiet in the day and I use that for applications. I'm up at seven, do an hour of the gym because it keeps my head straight, and then apply and follow up until lunch. Afternoons I call small firms directly, which most people don't do, and Sunday I go to Mass and see my girlfriend Anja, who's a nurse at the hospital. I studied finance at Marlowe University, top of my year, and interned at a shipping agent's accounts office and a building society. I've been out for five months, with 42,000 of debt and no offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's reasonable and I'd carry on. Things go on as normal and most of what's said about AI is noise. I'd tell my mates that a person still has to turn up and do the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it changes nothing for me, and that's the problem. I'm 42,000 in debt and not working, and in Gannet Bay the firms that hire a graduate in finance you can count on one hand. If it's all as normal, I'm stuck in the line like everyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on phoning firms, because a direct call to a managing director got me both of my interviews. I'd also apply for sales and account roles in the shipping and building trades, since they'd lead to finance. And I'd keep working weekend shifts on the docks if they offer them, because the pay is decent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit knocked about. I keep going, but I'd like to be able to tell Anja I've got something to offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You phone small firms directly. How does that go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly it's polite and a bit surprised. Two firms said to send in my CV and one said come in and talk, which is how I got the interview at the shipping agent. A person answering the phone is still more likely to say yes than an online form.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is the waiting affecting your plans with Anja?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We want to marry, but we've put it off. I'd like to do it right, with my own income and a place of our own, and I can't until I have a steady wage. Anja says it's fine, but I can tell she'd like a date.

say: Most of what's said about AI is **noise**, and a person still has to turn up and do the work.
think: It changes nothing for me, and that's the **problem**: 42,000 in debt and no work.
Gannet Bay has about five firms that hire finance **graduates**.
do: Keep phoning **small firms** directly, since a call to a managing director got both my interviews.
Apply for sales and account roles in shipping and **building trades**.
feel: **Knocked about**: I keep going, but I want something to offer Anja.
S0.quote: A person answering the phone is still more likely to say yes than an online form.
fieldNote: Direct **phone calls** are his edge, and they have already got him interviews.
Debt and the lack of local firms are the **real** weight, not AI.
Wedding plans with Anja are on **hold** until he has steady pay.

steps.text: Phone five small firms every morning and ask for a manager
Apply for sales and account roles in shipping
Take weekend shifts at the docks
Hold the wedding date until I have a steady wage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real, and the sensible thing is to learn it, not complain. I'd say to my mates that the market sorts it out and people who adapt do well. And I'd say it'd be a mistake to expect handouts from anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a worry. The accounts office I interned in had a lot of invoice entry and matching, and a program does that in seconds. Without those junior jobs, firms are asking for more from people with no experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get better at the tools, going from now and then to daily. I'd take an evening course in data analysis and an Excel certificate. I'd also look at roles that involve customers and money, like loan advice at a building society, because people still want to talk to someone about a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I feel I could do something about it, which helps. Anja's job at the hospital is safe, which also takes a little of the pressure off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI tools now and then. Where do they help you and where not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It helps me with Excel formulas and checking my reports, and it's useless at telling me what a client needs. I've caught it making up figures, so I check everything twice, which probably defeats the point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the shipping agent's partner who hires people?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him that I know the old way and the new way, and that I'm the sort who learns quickly. I'd tell him I'd work for a modest wage for the first year, since I'm there to learn. A firm should take a chance on that.

say: It's real, so the sensible thing is to **learn** it, not complain.
The market sorts it out, and expecting **handouts** would be a mistake.
think: The accounts office I interned in did lots of invoice **matching**, which a program does in seconds.
Anja's hospital job is **safe**, which takes pressure off.
do: Use AI **daily** instead of now and then.
Take an evening **data analysis** course and an Excel certificate.
Look at **loan advice** at a building society, where people still want a person.
feel: **Uneasy**, but doing something about it helps.
S1.quote: I've caught it making up figures, so I check everything twice, which probably defeats the point.
fieldNote: Pushes **self-reliance** and learning, in line with his views on handouts.
Anja's safe nursing job is a **cushion** he mentions without being asked.
Offers a modest first-year **wage** to earn a chance.

steps.text: Use an AI assistant every day on practice accounts
Take an evening Excel and data analysis course
Apply for loan adviser roles at building societies
Offer a modest first-year wage to a small firm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening and nobody's ready, but we can't just wait for someone to fix it. I'd say we need to look after our own families and communities, with churches and clubs helping the people who lose out. I'd say that the government should keep out of the way of people who build things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm scared, honestly. The work I've trained for goes first, and I'd have two years at most to get into it. I'd probably never get my career started, and Anja's pay alone wouldn't carry two of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any work at all, starting with the docks, and I'd move in with Anja's family if it saved rent. I'd retrain for something hands-on, probably in the port, like crane or forklift operation, since those hold out three years longer. I'd put everything towards the debt, and I'd ask the church for a bit of help finding work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A knot in my stomach, and I'd keep it from Anja as long as I could. I'd probably fail at that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years. What happens to the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring it forward, if anything. If everything's changing, I'd rather be married and sharing the load than waiting for a good moment. We'd do it small, in the parish, and not spend any money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take help from anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From family and the parish, yes, and gladly. From the state, only if it's connected to work, like a place on a training course. I'd rather earn it than be given it.

say: It's frightening and nobody is ready, but we can't wait for someone to **fix** it.
Families and **parishes** should look after the people who lose out.
think: The work I trained for goes **first**, and I'd have two years at most.
Anja's pay alone wouldn't carry **two** of us.
do: Take any work at all, starting at the **docks**.
Retrain for **forklift** or crane operation, which holds out longer.
Put everything at the **debt** and ask the parish for help finding work.
feel: A **knot** in my stomach, which I'd try to hide from Anja.
S2.quote: If everything's changing, I'd rather be married and sharing the load than waiting for a good moment.
fieldNote: Fear leads him to **family** plans, not away from them: marry sooner.
Accepts help from parish and family but wants state support **tied to work**.
Targets **port** jobs that robots reach later.

steps.text: Train for forklift or crane operation at the port
Bring the wedding forward and keep it small in the parish
Take any dock work from the first month
Ask the parish to help me find work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long enough warning to do something about it. I'd say that businesses and training schemes should get ready now, and that we shouldn't wait for politicians. I'd tell my friends to put their effort in early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I could manage, which surprises me. If I started a job within the year, I'd have three or four years' experience before the thinking work goes. Then Anja and I would have time to build a base for a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first decent finance job and learn their systems. I'd pay 500 a month at the loan, and I'd save a bit for the wedding, which we'd hold in the second year. I'd also get a hands-on skill on the side, like a forklift licence, so I'm not dependent on a desk job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cautiously hopeful. A date for the wedding makes it feel real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years. What would you do first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, find the job, because everything else follows from a wage. I'd phone the firms again, now with a better approach, since I've learned what works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a good first firm be like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small family firm where the owner teaches you. Somewhere I can see the whole business and not only one box. That sort of place needs someone loyal, and I'm loyal.

say: Five years is a long enough warning to do something about it, and we shouldn't wait for **politicians**.
I'd tell friends to put their effort in **early**.
think: I could manage, which surprises me: a job this year gives three or four years of **experience**.
Anja and I would have time to build a base for a **family**.
do: Take the first decent finance job and learn the **systems**.
Pay **500** a month at the loan and save a bit for the wedding in year two.
Get a forklift **licence** on the side as a hands-on fallback.
feel: Cautiously **hopeful**: a date for the wedding makes it feel real.
S3.quote: A small family firm where the owner teaches you. Somewhere I can see the whole business and not only one box.
fieldNote: Time lets him build **family** and career together, with a date for the wedding.
Keeps a hands-on skill as **insurance** even in the better case.
Describes the kind of employer he wants, rooted in **loyalty**.

steps.text: Take the first decent finance job and learn the firm's systems
Pay 500 a month at the loan
Set the wedding for the second year
Get a forklift licence as a hands-on fallback

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, and everyone should use it well. I'd say that we should look after our families and not leave them to be surprised. I'd be happy to talk about it at the parish hall or with the lads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly settled. I could get a job and qualify, clear the loan and be a father by thirty. If the work changes later, I'd have the skills and savings to handle it, and Anja's nursing keeps us steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a first finance job, qualify for the professional exams and clear the loan in about six years. We'd marry in year two or three and aim for a small house in Gannet Bay by thirty. I'd use AI tools more as they become normal, since I use them a bit already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like having the wind behind you for a change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, how do you picture your life?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I picture a house with a small garden, a child or two, and me working at a firm where I've risen a bit. Anja's still nursing, which will be steady, and we're near both our families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your younger sister?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my sister to do something that lets her stand on her own, and to learn how to use these tools without leaning on them. And I'd tell my sister not to borrow more than she can see her way to paying back.

say: Ten years is plenty of time, so we should look after our **families** and not leave them surprised.
I'd happily talk about it at the **parish hall**.
think: I feel fairly settled: a job, a qualification, the loan **cleared** and a family by thirty.
do: Take a first finance job, pass the **exams** and clear the loan in six years.
Marry in year two or three and aim for a small **house** by thirty.
Use AI tools more as they become **normal**.
feel: **Calm**, like having the wind behind you for a change.
S4.quote: I'd tell my sister not to borrow more than she can see her way to paying back.
fieldNote: The easiest scenario for him, because his **family** plans fit the timeline.
Anja's nursing job is a **steady** base.

steps.text: Take a first finance job and study for professional exams

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two year one. It'd take my job before I've had it, and it'd put off everything with Anja. What would help is training that comes with a wage, local firms willing to take a chance on a graduate and a bit of patience from the lender.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe that I don't think the world owes me anything. I want to work and look after my own. I'd just like one person to open the door and let me show what I can do.

headlineQuote: I don't think the world owes me anything. I want to work and look after my own.
portrait: Karl is 23, top of his finance class, in a **shared room** in Gannet Bay with 42,000 of debt.
He is traditional and churchgoing, believes in work over handouts, and plans around his girlfriend Anja, a nurse.
He uses AI tools sometimes, checks them carefully and favours a **steady** step-by-step approach.
His mood eases as the clock slows, because his wedding and family plans fit a longer runway.
biggestWorry: The **2028** scenario, because it would end his career before it began and delay his wedding.
whatWouldHelp: **Training with a wage**, local firms willing to take a chance on him and patience from the lender.
